English Language
1.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “my strange old book collector... his sharp, wizened face... wedged under his
right arm [books],” and “When I turned again, Sherlock Holmes was standing smiling at me,” and
“I have given you a serious shock by my unnecessarily dramatic reappearance,”
Passage - 1: 100-Word Summary
The passage describes Dr. Watson’s investigation of a mysterious house, which is interrupted by
the arrival of an elderly book collector. During their conversation, the visitor makes an unusually
precise remark, prompting Watson to momentarily turn away. When he looks back, the old man
has vanished and is replaced by Sherlock Holmes, whom Watson believed to be dead. Overcome
with shock, Watson faints and later regains consciousness to find Holmes calmly explaining his
return. The scene highlights the stark contrast between Watson’s emotional reaction and Holmes’s
composed demeanor, reinforcing the theme that appearances can be deceptive and reality may
differ from perception.
Explanation: (A) Watson’s emotional reaction is exaggerated because he has misunderstood
Holmes’s calm and controlled return.
This option is not supported when we examine Watson’s reaction closely. The lines “I rose to my
feet, stared at him... and... I must have fainted” and later “Is it really you?... can it indeed be that
you are alive?” show that Watson’s response stems from shock at Holmes’s presumed death, not
from any misunderstanding of Holmes’s behavior. Further, Holmes himself says, “J had no idea
that you would be so affected,” which acknowledges the intensity but does not suggest that Watson
has misinterpreted the situation. Importantly, Watson correctly recognizes Holmes immediately
after the disguise is removed. Therefore, the issue is not exaggeration due to confusion, but a
natural reaction to an extraordinary event. Holmes’s remark about “appearances” refers to
disguise and deception, not Watson’s emotional state.
(B) The situation is more complex than it seems, as Holmes’s apparent death and reappearance
involve deliberate concealment.
This option is directly supported by multiple lines in the passage. Initially, the visitor is described
as “my strange old book collector... his sharp, wizened face... wedged under his right arm [books],”
which establishes a deceptive appearance. The turning point occurs when “When I turned again,
Sherlock Holmes was standing smiling at me,” clearly revealing that the earlier appearance was
false. Additionally, Watson’s question, “Js it possible that you succeeded in climbing out of that
awful abyss?” confirms that Holmes was believed dead, reinforcing the idea of a larger deception.
Holmes’s own remark, “I have given you a serious shock by my unnecessarily dramatic
reappearance,” further indicates that this was a planned concealment. Thus, “appearances are
deceptive” refers to both his disguise and his supposed death—making this the most textually
grounded interpretation.
(C) Watson’s physical weakness after fainting has caused him to misinterpret Holmes’s presence
and identity.

Although this option draws on a real event, the lines contradict its conclusion. The passage states,
“when it cleared I found... Holmes was bending over my chair,” indicating that Watson regains
clarity after fainting. Immediately after, he says, “Holmes!/... Is it really you?’—this is not
confusion but a request for confirmation due to disbelief. There is no line suggesting that Watson
mistakes Holmes for someone else or misidentifies him. On the contrary, Holmes speaks in a “well-
remembered voice,” reinforcing correct recognition. The fainting episode is followed by physical
recovery (“collar-ends undone... taste of brandy”), not cognitive distortion. Therefore, Watson’s
perception is reliable once he regains consciousness. Holmes’s statement about deceptive
appearances relates to his disguise, not to any misinterpretation caused by Watson’s physical
condition.
(D) The dramatic nature of Holmes’s return has created confusion, making the moment appear
more significant than it truly is.
This option misreads the tone of Holmes’s statement. While Holmes admits, “J have given you a
serious shock by my unnecessarily dramatic reappearance,” this line only acknowledges the manner
of his return, not its importance. The surrounding lines indicate that the event is genuinely
significant: Watson exclaims, “to think that you—you of all men—should be standing in my study,”
highlighting the magnitude of Holmes’s survival. Moreover, the earlier transformation—from
“strange old book collector” to Holmes—demonstrates deliberate deception, not trivial drama.
There is no suggestion in the text that the situation is less important than it appears. Instead, the
passage reveals that reality (Holmes alive, disguised) is more complex than surface impressions.
Thus, the confusion arises from hidden truth, not from exaggerated significance.
2.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “a grey mist swirled before my eyes,” indicating visual disorientation. This is
followed by “when it cleared I found my collar-ends undone and the tingling after-taste of brandy
upon my lips,”
Explanation: (A) Lingering physical disorientation shaping his perception, as he relies on sensory
details before fully processing Holmes’s presence.
This option is supported by the sequence of lines immediately after Watson regains consciousness.
The passage states, “a grey mist swirled before my eyes,” indicating visual disorientation. This is
followed by “when it cleared I found my collar-ends undone and the tingling after-taste of brandy
upon my lips,” which focuses on physical sensations rather than emotional clarity. These details
show that Watson is initially grounded in bodily awareness, not immediate emotional processing.
Only after this sensory recovery does he register Holmes’s presence (“Holmes was bending over my
chair’), and then react verbally. The question specifically asks about the immediate post-
consciousness state, and these lines clearly establish that Watson is first disoriented and
physically aware before emotionally responding. Hence, (A) accurately captures the temporal
priority of physical sensation over emotional reaction.
(B) Overwhelming astonishment mixed with disbelief, as he instantly seeks confirmation of
Holmes’s survival.
This option is partially correct but fails due to timing. The lines “Holmes/... Is it really you?... can
it indeed be that you are alive?” and “I can hardly believe my eyes” clearly reflect astonishment and
disbelief. However, these occur after Watson has regained composure from his physical state. The
passage first emphasizes sensory recovery—‘grey mist,” » “collar-ends undone,” “taste of brandy’—

before any emotional expression appears. The use of the word “instantly” in the option makes it
inaccurate, as Watson does not immediately express disbelief upon regaining consciousness; there
is an intermediate stage of physical awareness. Therefore, while the emotion described is valid for
a later moment, it does not correspond to the initial condition asked in the question. This makes
(B) a strong but incorrect distractor.
(C) Rapid emotional recovery marked by composure, as he quickly accepts the situation without
confusion or hesitation.
This option is contradicted by multiple lines that highlight Watson’s continued confusion and
emotional intensity. After recovering, Watson exclaims, “Is it really you?” and “I can hardly believe
my eyes,” which clearly indicate hesitation and disbelief rather than composure. Furthermore, the
earlier physical description—‘“grey mist swirled before my eyes’—suggests that recovery is neither
rapid nor smooth. There is no textual evidence that Watson “quickly accepts” the situation;
instead, he repeatedly seeks confirmation. The presence of strong exclamatory language and
questioning directly contradicts the idea of calm acceptance. Thus, this option fails because it
imposes a level of rational control and emotional stability that is not supported by the passage.
Watson’s response is gradual and uncertain, not immediate and composed.
(D) Suppressed emotional reaction driven by restraint, as he avoids expressing shock despite the
unexpected encounter.
This option is directly refuted by Watson’s explicit and intense reaction in the passage. Far from
suppressing emotion, Watson openly expresses shock through both physical and verbal responses.
He faints earlier (“J must have fainted”), and upon recovery, he exclaims, “Holmes!” followed by
multiple incredulous questions. The line “J can hardly believe my eyes” further reinforces that he is
not restraining his emotions but actively articulating them. There is no indication of emotional
control or deliberate suppression; instead, the passage portrays an involuntary and overwhelming
reaction. Therefore, this option contradicts the textual evidence by suggesting restraint where the
passage clearly shows expressive shock. The emotional intensity is explicit, not concealed, making
(D) an incorrect interpretation.
Answer: A
Reference Line: my strange old book collector... his sharp, wizened face... wedged under his
right arm, “When I turned again, Sherlock Holmes was standing smiling at me,” and “I must have
fainted,” followed by “Is it really you?” and “can it indeed be that you are alive?”
Explanation: (A) To describe how Holmes disguised himself and revealed his identity to Watson.
This option is directly supported by the central sequence of events in the passage. The visitor is
first introduced as “my strange old book collector... his sharp, wizened face... wedged under his
right arm [books]”, establishing the disguise. The turning point occurs when Watson notes, “When
I turned again, Sherlock Holmes was standing smiling at me,” which reveals that the old man and
Holmes are the same person. The rest of the passage focuses on Watson’s reaction: “J must have
fainted,” followed by “Is it really you?” and “can it indeed be that you are alive?” These lines show
that the passage is structured around the disguise — revelation — emotional response sequence.
No other theme is developed with equal emphasis. Therefore, the primary purpose is to narrate
Holmes’s concealment and dramatic reappearance.
(B) To explain the architectural features of the house at Park Lane in detail.

This option is incorrect because the description of the house is brief and serves only as background.
The passage mentions, “The house was separated from the street by a low wall and railing... it was
perfectly easy... to get into the garden,” and “the window was entirely inaccessible.” These details
help establish Watson’s initial confusion about the case but are not developed further. After this
short description, the narrative shifts completely to the arrival of the book collector and Holmes’s
revelation. Since the architectural details occupy only the opening lines and are not the focus of
the passage, they cannot represent its primary purpose. They function merely as context for
Watson’s investigation, not as the main subject of discussion.
(C) To highlight Watson’s daily routine and his interactions with visitors.
This option is not supported because the passage does not depict a routine or recurring pattern in
Watson’s life. While it does include an interaction with a visitor—‘the maid entered to say that a
person desired to see me’—this is a singular, significant event, not part of a habitual routine. The
visitor himself is extraordinary, as he turns out to be Holmes in disguise. Additionally, Watson’s
reaction—‘I must have fainted” and “Is it really you?’—indicates that this is an unusual and
emotionally charged moment, not an everyday occurrence. There are no references to repeated
activities or typical daily behavior. Hence, the passage is focused on a specific dramatic incident,
not on Watson’s routine or general interactions.
(D) To discuss the challenges of investigating a difficult criminal case.
This option is incorrect because the investigative element is only briefly introduced and not
developed. The opening lines describe Watson’s confusion: “did little to clear up the problem” and
the difficulty posed by the “inaccessible” window. However, this thread is quickly abandoned as the
narrative shifts to the arrival of the disguised visitor. There is no further discussion of suspects,
evidence, or investigative strategy. Instead, the focus moves entirely to Holmes’s reappearance and
Watson’s reaction. Since the passage does not continue exploring the case or its challenges, it
cannot be said to primarily discuss investigation. The mention of the problem serves only as an
initial setup, not the main purpose of the passage.
4.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “his sharp, wizened face peering out from a frame of white hair.”
Explanation: (A) Pale and weakened due to prolonged illness or physical exhaustion.
This option is not supported by the descriptive context of the line. The phrase “his sharp, wizened
face peering out from a frame of white hair” emphasizes age and facial texture, not illness. There is
no reference anywhere in the passage to the man being sick, fatigued, or physically weak. In fact,
he is active enough to carry “a dozen [books]... wedged under his right arm” and engage in
conversation, which contradicts the idea of exhaustion. The word “wizened” is paired with “sharp,”
suggesting a defined, aged appearance, not a weakened or unhealthy condition. Therefore,
interpreting “wizened” as “pale and weakened” introduces a meaning (illness) that is absent from
the text. This makes (A) a plausible but incorrect inference based on stereotype rather than textual
evidence.
(B) Thin and slightly shrivelled in appearance due to old age.
This option is best supported by the line “his sharp, wizened face peering out from a frame of white
hair.” The presence of “white hair” clearly signals old age, and “wizened” in this context describes
the effect of aging on the face, typically involving wrinkles and slight shrinkage. The adjective
“sharp” complements this by suggesting that the features are narrow or defined, not full or smooth.

There is no indication of illness or emotional expression; the focus is purely on physical appearance
shaped by age. Additionally, the man’s active behavior—walking, carrying books, speaking
fluently—indicates that the description is visual rather than functional. Thus, “thin and slightly
shrivelled due to old age” aligns precisely with both the immediate description and the broader
context, making (B) the most accurate interpretation.
(C) Expressive and alert with signs of intelligence and awareness.
This option is a close distractor because of the nearby word “sharp,” which can suggest intelligence
or alertness. However, the phrase “sharp, wizened face” functions as a combined physical
description, not a comment on mental ability. The passage does not describe the man’s expressions,
reactions, or intellect in this line; instead, it focuses on how his face looks. While the character
later speaks intelligently about books, that is separate from the meaning of “wizened.” The word
specifically relates to aged appearance, not liveliness or awareness. Therefore, interpreting it as
“expressive and alert” misreads the adjective by shifting from physical texture (wrinkled, aged) to
mental qualities (intelligence). This makes (C) incorrect, though it may tempt readers who rely too
heavily on the word “sharp” without considering the full phrase.
(D) Angular and narrow with sharply defined facial features.
This option captures part of the description but misses the key nuance of “wizened.” The word
“sharp” in the line may support the idea of angular or defined features, but “wizened” specifically
adds the dimension of aging—wrinkling and slight shrinkage. The phrase “frame of white hair”
reinforces that the description is tied to age, not merely shape. While an angular face could belong
to someone of any age, “wizened” restricts the meaning to an aged, weathered appearance.
Therefore, (D) is incomplete: it accounts for structure but ignores the effect of time on the face,
which is central to the word’s meaning. This makes it a strong distractor, as it partially aligns with
“sharp,” but ultimately fails to incorporate the full contextual clue provided in the passage.
5.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “I had no idea that you would be so affected.” And “Is it really you? Can it indeed
be that you are alive?”
Explanation: (A) a composed engagement with Holmes’s apology, where Watson attempts to
process the remark before reacting further.
This option is not supported by the actual wording of Watson’s response. Holmes’s statement is: “J
owe you a thousand apologies... I had no idea that you would be so affected.” A composed
engagement would involve Watson acknowledging or responding to this apology directly. However,
Watson immediately exclaims, “Holmes! Is it really you? Can it indeed be that you are alive?” This
reaction is abrupt and emotionally charged, not composed or reflective. There is no evidence of
Watson pausing to process Holmes’s remark or responding in a measured manner. Instead, his
response bypasses the apology entirely and moves straight to disbelief about Holmes’s survival.
Therefore, this option incorrectly attributes calmness and logical engagement where the text
clearly shows emotional urgency and surprise.
(B) a restrained acknowledgment of Holmes’s explanation, followed by a gradual shift toward
emotional acceptance.
This option misrepresents both the tone and structure of Watson’s response. First, Watson does
not acknowledge Holmes’s statement at all—there is no reference to the apology or explanation.
Instead, his response begins immediately with “Holmes!” followed by two urgent questions: “Is it

really you? Can it indeed be that you are alive?” These lines indicate intense emotional shock
rather than restraint. Additionally, there is no “gradual shift” visible; the reaction is instantaneous
and strongly expressive. Words like “really” and “indeed” emphasize disbelief, not acceptance. The
absence of any transitional or calming language further contradicts the idea of emotional
moderation. Hence, this option fails because it introduces qualities—restraint and gradual
acceptance—that are not supported by the textual evidence.
(C) a continuation of the same conversational thread, directly addressing Holmes’s apology with a
relevant clarification.
This option is incorrect because Watson’s response does not continue the same conversational
thread initiated by Holmes. Holmes speaks about Watson being “affected” and offers an apology for
his dramatic reappearance. A continuation would require Watson to address this—perhaps by
explaining his reaction or responding to the apology. However, Watson’s reply—‘“TIs it really you?...
can it indeed be that you are alive?’—shifts entirely to a different concern: Holmes’s survival.
There is no linguistic or thematic connection to Holmes’s apology in Watson’s response. The
absence of keywords or ideas related to “apology” or “reaction” shows a clear break in the
conversational flow. Thus, rather than continuing the thread, Watson redirects it, making this
option inconsistent with the passage.
(D) a deviation from Holmes’s statement, as Watson shifts focus to Holmes’s unexpected survival
rather than the apology itself.
This option is directly supported by comparing the two lines of dialogue. Holmes’s statement
focuses on Watson’s reaction: “IJ had no idea that you would be so affected.” However, Watson’s
reply—‘Is it really you? Can it indeed be that you are alive?’—does not address this point at all.
Instead, it introduces a new focus: Holmes’s survival after being presumed dead. The absence of
any reference to the apology indicates a clear shift in conversational direction. Additionally, the
urgency and repetition in Watson’s questions show that his attention is fully occupied by the shock
of Holmes being alive. Therefore, Watson’s response is best understood as a deviation, where he
ignores the original statement and redirects the conversation to a more pressing concern.
6.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “My dear Watson... I had not anticipated that my reappearance would affect you
so strongly.” And “a grey mist swirled before my eyes, and I lost all sense of awareness”
Explanation: (A) Watson’s emotional shock contrasts with Holmes’s calm and calculated
composure — Correct
This option accurately captures the central tension between the two characters. Watson reacts
with intense emotion and disbelief—he is “astonished,” physically overwhelmed, and even loses
consciousness (“a grey mist swirled before my eyes, and I lost all sense of awareness”). His response
is driven by shock, relief, and confusion at Holmes’s unexpected return. In contrast, Holmes
remains composed and controlled throughout. Even after revealing himself, he speaks calmly: “My
dear Watson... I had not anticipated that my reappearance would affect you so strongly.” His tone
is measured, almost clinical, and he even anticipates Watson’s reaction analytically. This
contrast—emotion vs rational composure—forms the core tension of the scene. Therefore, option
(a) best reflects the passage.
(B) Holmes’s confusion about the situation contrasts with Watson’s clear understanding of events
— Incorrect

This option reverses the actual dynamic between the two characters. Holmes is never shown to be
confused; rather, he is fully aware and in control of the situation, having orchestrated the disguise
and reveal. His calm demeanor and explanatory tone indicate clarity, not confusion. On the other
hand, Watson is the one who is disoriented and struggling to process events. His reaction—losing
consciousness and later questioning whether he can “trust [his] senses”—demonstrates uncertainty
and emotional overwhelm. Thus, this option incorrectly assigns confusion to Holmes and clarity to
Watson, making it inconsistent with the passage.
(C) Watson’s suspicion of Holmes conflicts with Holmes’s attempt to justify his actions — Incorrect
While Watson is surprised and emotionally shaken, he does not express suspicion toward Holmes.
His reaction is one of disbelief and relief rather than doubt or mistrust. He exclaims, “Is it truly
you? Can you indeed be alive?,” which reflects astonishment, not suspicion. Similarly, Holmes does
not attempt to justify his actions in this moment; instead, he offers an apology for the dramatic
effect of his return. There is no argument or defensive explanation occurring between them.
Therefore, this option introduces a conflict that does not exist in the passage and is incorrect.
(D) Holmes’s urgency to explain events contrasts with Watson’s reluctance to engage in discussion
— Incorrect
This option misrepresents both characters’ behavior. Holmes does not display urgency; in fact, he
remains calm and even pauses before explaining further (“He paused”). His approach is measured
rather than rushed. Watson, on the other hand, is eager to understand what has happened. He
actively questions Holmes and expresses a strong desire to know the truth: “Did you escape that
dreadful abyss?” This shows engagement, not reluctance. The tension is not about willingness to
communicate but about emotional contrast. Hence, this option is incorrect.
7.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “responsibility carried in the name of their honour”, “no thought of surrender
found place among them”, and “the defenders could only endure.” And “not merely a battle, but a
testament” and “they fought not for survival, but for something greater than themselves.”
Passage - 2: 100-Word Summary
The passage recounts the Battle of Saragarhi (1897), where twenty-one soldiers defended an
isolated post against a vastly larger force. Despite being surrounded and cut off from
reinforcements, they chose to resist rather than surrender, driven by duty and honour. The
attackers launched repeated assaults and eventually breached the post, but the defenders
continued to fight with unwavering resolve. Even as defeat became inevitable, communication with
nearby forts continued, symbolizing discipline and commitment. Ultimately, all defenders fell, but
their sacrifice transformed the event from a mere military engagement into a lasting symbol of
courage, resilience, and devotion to a cause greater than individual survival.
Explanation: (A) The geographical and military importance of Saragarhi as a communication
post.
This option is partially supported by the opening description: “isolated, exposed, yet crucial” and
“served as a vital communication link.” However, these lines only establish the setting. The
passage quickly shifts to ideas like “upholding duty,” “no thought of surrender,” and “they fought
not for survival, but for something greater than themselves.” These lines clearly move beyond
geography into values. The communication role is mentioned again through “messages continued to
flash,” but even that becomes symbolic when Gurmukh Singh joins the fight. Thus, while

geography and function are present, they are not sustained as the main focus. The passage is not
explaining terrain or logistics in detail, but using them as a backdrop. Therefore, this option
captures only an introductory idea and misses the dominant theme of sacrifice and patriotism.
(B) The heroic resistance of a small group of soldiers reflecting duty, sacrifice, and patriotism.
This option is consistently supported across the passage. Early lines such as “responsibility carried
in the name of their honour” introduce duty. The middle sections reinforce this with “no thought of
surrender found place among them” and “the defenders could only endure.” The climax intensifies
the theme through “not merely a battle, but a testament” and “they fought not for survival, but for
something greater than themselves.” These lines clearly indicate that the focus is not on tactics or
geography but on values—courage, sacrifice, and patriotism. Even the final line—“a lasting
expression of courage, honour’—cements this interpretation. Since the passage consistently
develops this idea from beginning to end, (B) accurately captures the central and sustained theme.
(C) The tactical superiority of tribal forces over isolated military positions.
This option is misleading because it overemphasizes the attackers. While the passage mentions “a
massive tribal force... returned in waves,” this is used to highlight the defenders’ disadvantage, not
to analyse the attackers’ superiority. The narrative focus remains on the defenders: “repelled the
first assault,” “their numbers steadily thinning,” and “none yielded.” There is no discussion of
tactics, planning, or strategic brilliance of the attacking forces. Instead, their numerical strength
serves as a contrast to the defenders’ courage. Thus, this option incorrectly shifts attention away
from the core theme. The passage is not about evaluating military superiority but about moral
strength under overwhelming pressure.
(D) The role of communication systems in determining outcomes of frontier battles.
This option is based on lines like “heliographic communication” and “messages continued to flash to
Fort Lockhart.” However, these references are limited and supportive in nature. The passage does
not analyse communication systems or their broader impact. Instead, communication becomes
symbolic when “Gurmukh Singh sent his final signal and chose to join the fight,” shifting focus
from system to sacrifice. The narrative does not argue that communication determined the
outcome; in fact, the post falls despite it. Therefore, this option misinterprets a supporting detail
as the main idea. The true emphasis lies on human courage, not technological function.
8.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “in a region where visibility itself was a challenge.”
Explanation: (A) It was geographically difficult, making communication both essential and
challenging.
This option is best supported by the line “in a region where visibility itself was a challenge.” The
phrase directly indicates environmental or geographical difficulty, particularly terrain or
atmospheric conditions that obstruct clear sight. This is further reinforced by earlier descriptors
such as “isolated, exposed,” which establish that Saragarhi was located in a harsh and vulnerable
setting. Since heliographic communication depends entirely on visibility, the difficulty mentioned
in the line implies that maintaining communication would be both challenging and crucial. The
passage does not merely describe a location but highlights a condition that makes the post
strategically important. Thus, the option correctly integrates both aspects—difficulty and
necessity—without adding external assumptions. It reflects a precise reading of the line in context,
making it the most accurate interpretation of Saragarhi’s situation.

(B) It was technologically advanced compared to surrounding military posts.
This option is not supported by the passage because the line does not indicate any form of
technological superiority. The mention of “heliographic communication” might appear technical,
but the focus of the sentence is on limitation rather than advancement. The phrase “visibility itself
was a challenge” suggests that the environment made communication difficult, not that the
technology used was superior or innovative. There is no comparison with other military posts, nor
is there any indication that Saragarhi possessed better equipment or more advanced systems.
Instead, the passage presents heliography as a necessity in a constrained setting. Therefore,
interpreting this line as evidence of technological advancement introduces an idea that is not
present in the text. This makes option (B) a misreading of the context, as it shifts attention from
environmental difficulty to unsupported technological superiority.
(C) It lacked trained personnel capable of maintaining communication systems.
This option incorrectly attributes the challenge mentioned in the line to human incapability rather
than environmental difficulty. The phrase “visibility itself was a challenge” clearly refers to
external conditions, not to the competence of the soldiers. In fact, the passage provides evidence to
the contrary: “messages continued to flash to Fort Lockhart even as the walls began to fall.” This
indicates that the personnel were highly trained and capable of maintaining communication under
extreme pressure. There is no suggestion anywhere in the passage that the defenders lacked skill
or efficiency. Instead, their ability to sustain communication despite worsening conditions
highlights their discipline and resilience. Therefore, this option misinterprets the source of
difficulty by shifting it from geography to human limitation, which is not supported by the text.
(D) It was strategically unimportant despite its communication function.
This option is directly contradicted by explicit statements in the passage. The opening lines
describe Saragarhi as “yet crucial” and emphasize that it “served as a vital communication link
between the two forts.” These phrases clearly establish its strategic importance. The line “visibility
itself was a challenge” does not reduce this importance; instead, it explains why the post was
necessary despite difficult conditions. The difficulty of maintaining communication actually
increases the value of the post, as it performs a critical function under constraints. There is no
indication that Saragarhi was insignificant; rather, the passage repeatedly reinforces its
importance through both description and action. Therefore, option (D) contradicts clear textual
evidence and misrepresents the role of the post within the narrative.
9.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “their numbers steadily thinning,” and “cut off from reinforcements, supplies,
and retreat,”
Explanation: (A) The defenders were unwilling to retaliate despite repeated attacks.
This option is contradicted by explicit evidence in the passage. The line in question—“the defenders
could only endure, their numbers steadily thinning’—must be read alongside earlier lines such as
“the defenders repelled the first assault.” This clearly shows that the defenders were actively
resisting and not passive. The word “endure” does not imply unwillingness to fight; rather, it
reflects their ability to continue resisting under pressure. Additionally, later lines like “none
yielded” further confirm their active participation and determination. If the defenders were
unwilling to retaliate, the passage would not highlight repeated resistance or the physical toll of

battle. Therefore, this option misinterprets “endure” as passivity, whereas the context shows active
resistance despite worsening conditions.
(B) The defenders were gradually losing strength without reinforcement.
This option is directly supported by the phrase “their numbers steadily thinning,” which clearly
indicates a reduction in manpower over time. This must be read in conjunction with the earlier
line “cut off from reinforcements, supplies, and retreat,” which establishes that no external support
was available. Together, these lines show a clear cause-and-effect relationship: as the battle
continues, losses increase, and there is no possibility of replenishment. The word “endure” further
suggests that the defenders are continuing despite this disadvantage, not because conditions are
improving. The passage consistently reinforces this idea of isolation and gradual weakening.
Therefore, this option accurately captures both the process (steady loss) and the condition (absence
of reinforcement), making it the most precise interpretation.
(C) The defenders chose to retreat slowly to conserve their resources.
There is no evidence in the passage to support the idea of retreat. In fact, the text explicitly
suggests the opposite through lines such as “no thought of surrender found place among them” and
“none yielded.” The phrase “could only endure” indicates that the defenders remained in position
despite increasing pressure, not that they withdrew strategically. Additionally, the description of
the final stages—where the defenders continue fighting even as their numbers diminish—further
contradicts any notion of retreat. If retreat had been part of their strategy, it would have been
mentioned explicitly, especially given the detailed narrative of the battle. Therefore, this option
introduces an idea that is neither stated nor implied in the passage and is inconsistent with the
defenders’ demonstrated resolve.
(D) The defenders were being replaced continuously by fresh troops.
This option is directly contradicted by the passage’s emphasis on isolation. The line “cut off from
reinforcements, supplies, and retreat” clearly establishes that no additional troops could reach
Saragarhi. The phrase “numbers steadily thinning” further reinforces that losses were not being
